lessons.title: Papers & Boards: Sources, Types & Properties
lessons.description: From wood pulp to finished sheet: sources, common types and working properties of paper and board.
lessons.content_html:
Where Paper and Board Come From

Paper and board begin as wood pulp — a slurry of cellulose fibres extracted from softwood trees such as pine and spruce. Timber is chipped, then either mechanically ground or chemically treated (the kraft process) to break the wood into individual fibres. Chemical pulping removes more lignin, producing a stronger, more durable sheet; mechanical pulping is cheaper but results in a weaker, more acidic paper that yellows over time. Alongside virgin wood pulp, the industry relies heavily on recycled fibre recovered from used newspapers, cardboard boxes and office paper. Recycled content reduces demand on forests and the energy needed to process raw timber.

Sustainable sourcing is increasingly important. The FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) certifies paper products whose raw materials come from forests managed to strict environmental, social and economic standards. FSC-certified paper guarantees that for every tree felled, replanting or natural regeneration takes place. Designers specifying paper for a product brief should always consider whether FSC certification is required by the client or demanded by the target market.

How Paper and Board Are Made

Pulp is mixed with large quantities of water to form a dilute slurry containing roughly 99% water. This slurry is sprayed onto a moving wire mesh (the Fourdrinier machine), where water drains through the mesh and the fibres begin to mat together. The wet web of fibres then passes through a series of press rollers that squeeze out more water, followed by heated drying cylinders that evaporate the remainder. The result is a continuous roll of paper. To make board, multiple plies of pulp are layered and pressed together while still wet, increasing thickness and rigidity. Coating with clay or chalk and calendering (pressing between smooth rollers) creates a smooth, printable surface.

Key Fact

Paper is measured in grams per square metre (GSM or g/m²). Below 170 g/m² is generally classed as paper; above 170 g/m² is classed as card or board. Typical photocopier paper is 80 g/m²; a cereal-box folding boxboard is around 280–350 g/m².

Common Papers and Their Uses

The paper family includes a wide range of specialist sheets, each engineered for a specific design or production purpose:

  • Cartridge paper — a thick, slightly textured paper (90–135 g/m²) used for hand drawing, sketching and painting. Its surface tooth holds pencil, ink and watercolour well.
  • Layout paper — lightweight and semi-transparent, allowing designers to trace and overlay ideas quickly during the initial design stages.
  • Tracing paper — highly transparent, used to copy drawings precisely or to create overlays that show different layers of a design separately.
  • Grid paper — pre-printed with squares, isometric dots or perspective grids to assist accurate technical drawing without specialist equipment.
  • Bleed-proof paper — specially coated so marker pen ink does not spread beyond the drawn line, giving sharp, clean edges in rendered design visuals.
  • Sugar paper — a rough, recycled-content paper available in a wide colour range, used for mounting, display work and craft activities.

Common Boards and Their Properties

Boards are stiffer, thicker and more rigid than papers. Each type is engineered for specific structural or commercial applications:

  • Corrugated card — a sandwich structure with a fluted (wavy) inner layer between two flat liner sheets. The flutes act as columns, giving excellent compressive strength and cushioning, ideal for transit packaging and product boxes.
  • Duplex board — a board with a bleached white top layer for printing and a grey recycled-fibre back. Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost. Used for food packaging, cereal boxes and cosmetics cartons where a high-quality printed surface is required at moderate cost.
  • Solid white board (SWB) — made entirely from virgin bleached chemical pulp, giving a brilliant white surface on both sides. Higher-grade and more expensive than duplex board; used for premium packaging where colour accuracy is critical.
  • Foil-lined board — a paper or board laminated to a thin aluminium foil layer on one side, providing a moisture and gas barrier. Used in food packaging (butter wrappers, confectionery cartons, coffee pouches) and drinks cartons.
  • Foam board — a polystyrene foam core sandwiched between two sheets of smooth paper. Extremely lightweight yet rigid; used for architectural models, point-of-sale displays and exhibition graphics.
  • Inkjet card — a smooth, coated card optimised for home or office inkjet printing, giving sharp colour reproduction. Common weight: 160–300 g/m².
  • Mount board — a thick, acid-free board (approximately 1,400 microns) available in many colours, used to frame and display artwork or photographs without yellowing over time.

Paper weight in GSM (grams per square metre) measures mass, not physical thickness — a dense coated paper can be heavier in GSM yet thinner than a bulkier uncoated sheet of the same GSM. For board, physical thickness is often quoted in microns (micrometres, µm) — one micron is one thousandth of a millimetre. A standard cereal box folding boxboard is around 280–350 g/m² and approximately 400–500 microns thick. When a designer specifies board for a packaging brief, both figures may be relevant: GSM determines postage cost and stiffness calculations, while micron thickness determines whether the net will fit together at scored folds.

Callipers measure board thickness in microns. A micrometer screw gauge gives precise readings to 1–2 microns. In a workshop, a simple rule of thumb is that 1 micron ≈ 1 g/m² for uncoated boards, but this ratio shifts once clay coating is applied.

Physical and Working Properties

When selecting a paper or board, designers must consider several key properties. Stiffness (resistance to bending) increases with thickness and with the grain direction of the fibres — paper is considerably stiffer when bent against the grain. Porosity affects ink absorption; coated boards absorb less ink, giving sharper printed images. Opacity describes how much light passes through; a high-opacity sheet prevents text from showing through to the reverse side. Whiteness influences perceived print quality; a brighter white base improves colour vibrancy. Tear resistance is highest parallel to the grain direction. Tensile strength measures resistance to being pulled apart; kraft paper, used for paper bags and envelopes, has high tensile strength due to long chemical pulp fibres.

Key Fact

Paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction) during manufacture. Paper and board fold more cleanly, crease more crisply and are stiffer along the grain. When cutting nets for packaging, the grain direction should run parallel to the longest fold lines to prevent cracking and produce a neater carton.

Ecological and Social Footprint

Paper production has significant environmental impacts. Pulp mills consume large quantities of water (up to 10 litres per sheet of A4) and energy, and the chemical bleaching process produces chlorine-based by-products if elemental chlorine is used. Modern mills increasingly use totally chlorine-free (TCF) or elemental chlorine-free (ECF) bleaching to reduce toxic effluent. Deforestation is a key concern: illegal logging for paper pulp destroys biodiversity and releases stored carbon. FSC certification and recycled-content labelling allow consumers and designers to make informed choices. Socially, paper mills in developing countries have faced criticism for poor working conditions and displacement of indigenous forest communities — ethical procurement policies address this by requiring supplier audits.

Recycled fibre uses significantly less water and energy than virgin pulp, and diverts waste from landfill. Each time a fibre is recycled, however, it shortens slightly, reducing the strength and quality of the resulting sheet. Recycled board typically has a grey or brown appearance, which is why duplex board uses a white virgin-pulp surface layer over a recycled grey back. High-quality printing generally requires a proportion of virgin fibre to maintain brightness and smoothness.

The ideal solution for most packaging applications is a mixed-content board: recycled fibre for the structural core layers where strength per unit weight matters less, and virgin or de-inked pulp for the outer printing surface. This approach balances environmental performance against the technical requirements of modern printing and surface finishing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to name or describe a paper or board, always include three elements: the name of the material, a key property (e.g. lightweight, stiff, transparent), and a specific use (e.g. cereal packaging, architectural models). Answers that name only the material without linking it to a property and purpose rarely score full marks on 3-mark or 4-mark questions. For sustainability questions, go beyond simply writing ‘it is recycled’ — state what that means in practice (reduced water use, shorter fibres, lower energy demand).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Paper and board are made from wood pulp or recycled fibre; FSC certification guarantees responsible forest management. Weight is measured in GSM and thickness in microns, and the two do not always correspond directly.
  • Common papers (cartridge, layout, tracing, bleed-proof, sugar) are selected for specific design and drawing tasks; common boards (corrugated, duplex, solid white, foil-lined, foam, mount) are chosen for packaging, modelling and display based on their structural and surface properties.
  • Fibre grain direction, stiffness, opacity, porosity and tensile strength are critical working properties. Recycled-content boards reduce environmental impact but sacrifice some printability; mixed-content boards balance both.

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper is manufactured from wood pulp.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- Wood is chipped and treated to separate cellulose fibres into a pulp slurry.
- The slurry is spread onto a moving wire mesh where water drains away and fibres mat together.
- The web passes through press rollers and heated drying cylinders to remove remaining moisture and form a continuous roll. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why grain direction is important when cutting and folding a net for a cardboard carton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- During manufacture, paper fibres align in the machine direction (grain direction).
- Paper and board are considerably stiffer when bent against the grain, so aligning the grain along the fold lines reduces the force needed to score and crease.
- Folding against the grain can crack the surface coating and weaken the structure of the carton.
- Specifying grain direction correctly during print finishing reduces waste and improves the quality of the assembled box. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging designer might choose duplex board rather than solid white board for a breakfast cereal box, considering both performance and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Duplex board has a white bleached top surface suitable for high-quality printing, meeting the visual requirements of cereal-box branding.
- The grey recycled-fibre back layer reduces raw material cost compared with solid white board, which uses 100% virgin chemical pulp.
- Using recycled fibre in the core layers reduces energy consumption and water use during manufacture, lowering the carbon footprint of the packaging.
- Solid white board offers superior whiteness and colour accuracy, which may be justified for premium products where brand colour precision is critical.
- For a budget cereal brand, the cost saving of duplex board outweighs the marginal loss in print quality; for a luxury brand, solid white board may be justified.
[6 marks - Mastering: Balanced comparison referencing both material performance and sustainability with application to the cereal box context. Secure: Performance and sustainability points made but comparison lacks full development. Developing: One board described well; limited comparison. Emerging: Basic identification only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using recycled fibre rather than virgin wood pulp in the manufacture of paper and board products.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
- Recycled fibre uses significantly less energy and water than processing virgin wood pulp, reducing the environmental impact of manufacture.
- Using recycled content diverts waste paper and board from landfill, extending the useful life of the raw material.
- Recycled-content products can carry on-pack environmental claims that appeal to environmentally conscious consumers and retail buyers.
- Reduces demand for virgin timber, helping to protect forests and the biodiversity they support.
Disadvantages:
- Each recycling cycle shortens the cellulose fibres, reducing tensile strength and making it harder to produce high-quality printing surfaces.
- Recycled board is typically grey or brown in colour; achieving a white surface requires a virgin-fibre top ply, adding cost and complexity.
- Ink contamination in recycled streams must be removed by de-inking, which adds a processing stage and produces sludge waste requiring disposal.
- The quality and availability of recycled fibre fluctuates with consumer recycling rates, making supply chains less predictable than virgin pulp sourcing.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages, linked to real design or manufacturing contexts. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance between sides. Emerging: One-sided response or very superficial points.]

lessons.title: Selecting Papers & Boards for a Purpose
lessons.description: Matching paper and board to a design brief: function, aesthetics, cost, stock forms and sustainability.
lessons.content_html:
Why Selection Matters

Choosing the wrong paper or board for a product leads to failure — a flimsy cereal carton that cannot survive stacking in a warehouse, a point-of-sale display that buckles under its own weight, or packaging whose surface absorbs ink and blurs the brand logo. Designers must balance several competing factors every time they specify a material: function (will it do the job?), aesthetics (does it look and feel right?), cost (is it within budget?), availability (can it be sourced in the right stock form?), and environmental and ethical considerations (is it sustainably sourced and responsibly produced?). These factors rarely point to the same material, so selection always involves a reasoned compromise.

Functional Requirements

The function of the final product sets the baseline specification. A pizza delivery box must resist heat and grease transfer; a corrugated single-wall board with a grease-resistant liner meets this need. A luxury chocolate box must convey premium quality; a solid white board with a matt laminate and foil-blocked logo achieves this. A stiffness requirement might rule out lightweight papers, while a need for moisture resistance immediately points toward coated or foil-lined boards. When reading a design brief, the first step is to identify these performance-critical properties and use them to narrow the material choices before considering cost or availability.

Aesthetic Requirements

Paper and board contribute significantly to a product’s perceived quality. A bright white, smooth surface makes colours appear vivid and saturated when printed; a cream, textured stock creates a premium, artisan impression. Whiteness and brightness are measured on standardised scales: solid white board (SWB) achieves the highest values, making it the default for luxury packaging and cosmetics. Touch matters too: uncoated boards feel warm and natural, while high-gloss laminated boards feel cool and slick. For point-of-sale displays, visual impact is paramount, so thicker boards, bold substrates and eye-catching surface finishes (metallic foil, UV spot varnish) are commonly specified even at higher cost.

Key Fact

Standard paper sizes follow the ISO A-series. A0 is 841 × 1,189 mm and has an area of exactly 1 m². Each size down halves the longer dimension: A1 is half of A0, A2 is half of A1, and so on. A3 (297 × 420 mm) and A4 (210 × 297 mm) are the most common in design work. Printers charge by sheet size, so understanding which standard size your net fits into directly affects production cost.

Cost and Availability

Raw material cost rises with fibre quality and surface treatment. Solid white board costs more than duplex board, which costs more than grey-back recycled board. Foil-lined board and specialist coatings add further expense. When a client specifies a tight unit cost for a product, the designer must find the cheapest material that still meets the performance and aesthetic specification. Availability is equally important: standard boards are held in stock by paper merchants in common sizes and weights; specialist boards may require a minimum order quantity or a lead time of several weeks. For small-batch or prototype runs, sticking to standard stock forms reduces cost and delay.

Matching Material to Product Type

Different product categories have well-established material conventions:

  • Packaging (food and consumer goods) — folding boxboard (duplex or SWB) for cartons; corrugated single or double wall for transit boxes; foil-lined board for products requiring a moisture or gas barrier (butter, coffee, ready meals).
  • Modelling — foam board for architectural models (light, easy to cut, rigid); grey-back mountboard for scaled mock-ups; corrugated card for protective inner packaging prototypes.
  • Graphics and print — coated art paper (135–200 g/m²) for magazines and brochures; uncoated cartridge (80–120 g/m²) for books and letterheads; high-gloss photo paper for photographic reproduction.
  • Point-of-sale (POS) displays — corrugated board for self-standing floor displays (strong and light); foam board for wall-mounted graphics (easily cut to shape); solid white board for premium counter-top displays.

Paper and board are available in several stock forms from merchants. Sheets are pre-cut to standard sizes (commonly A0, A1, SRA1, SRA2 and their multiples for commercial print). Reams (500 sheets) are the standard purchasing unit for office-grade paper. Rolls are used in continuous-feed production machinery such as rotary presses and corrugating lines. Designers specify material in these standard forms because non-standard sizes incur cutting charges and wastage. When developing a net (template) for packaging, a good designer positions the net on the sheet to minimise waste — a process called imposition.

For the A-series, the aspect ratio of every size is 1:√2. This means that two sheets of any A-size placed together form the next size up — two A4 sheets make one A3, two A3 sheets make one A2. This elegant property minimises offcuts when scaling artwork up or down and allows consistent scaling of designs without distortion.

Forces, Stresses and Stiffening Methods

Packaging must withstand a variety of forces during manufacture, transit and retail display. Compressive forces act downward when boxes are stacked; tensile forces act to pull walls apart when a filled box is lifted; shear forces occur at the glued joints when a carton is dropped. Boards are engineered to resist these stresses in several ways:

  • Corrugation — the fluted core of corrugated board acts as a series of arches, dramatically increasing compressive strength without adding significant weight. Single-wall corrugated board can resist pressures many times greater than a flat board of equal weight.
  • Lamination — bonding two or more plies of material together increases bending stiffness far more than adding the same total thickness as a single ply. Lamination can also combine a stiff structural layer with a printable surface layer and a functional barrier layer in a single sheet.
  • Grain direction — orienting the board so the machine direction (grain) runs parallel to the longest fold lines maximises stiffness in the direction where the packaging must resist bending under load.
Key Fact

The ISO A-series runs from A0 (1 m² area) down to A10. Each step halves the sheet: A4 is one-sixteenth of A0. All sizes share the same 1:√2 aspect ratio, so artwork scales perfectly without distortion between sizes. This is the international standard used across all Eduqas specification and design work.

Environmental and Ethical Selection Factors

Increasingly, client briefs specify minimum environmental standards for packaging materials. Specifying FSC-certified board demonstrates commitment to responsible forestry. Choosing recycled-content board reduces virgin fibre demand and associated carbon emissions. Selecting materials that are readily recyclable at end of life means the product can re-enter the material cycle — important for both regulatory compliance and consumer acceptance. Avoiding mixed-material boards (e.g. foil-laminated multi-layer cartons) where possible simplifies end-of-life recycling. Local sourcing reduces transport emissions. Ethical considerations include ensuring suppliers hold recognised certification (e.g. ISO 14001 environmental management) and do not source from regions with poor labour standards.

Foil-lined board bonds an aluminium layer to a paper substrate using adhesive. At end of life, separating the aluminium from the paper fibre is technically difficult and economically unattractive for most recycling facilities. As a result, most foil-lined cartons (drinks cartons, butter wrappers) end up in landfill or energy-from-waste incineration rather than material recycling. Some specialist facilities use hydro-pulping to separate the layers, but these are not widely available. This recyclability problem must be weighed against the functional benefit the foil provides — without it, many perishable foods would spoil much faster, increasing food waste.

Designers seeking a barrier function without the recyclability drawback may specify clay-coated board with a water-based moisture barrier, which is recyclable, or bio-based polymer coatings that are compostable under industrial conditions. These alternatives are less effective barriers than foil but represent a significant environmental improvement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Selection questions typically ask you to justify a material choice by linking it to the product’s functional and aesthetic requirements. Always use a PEE structure: state the Point (the material), provide the Evidence (its relevant property, e.g. high stiffness, moisture-resistant coating), and Explain how that property meets a specific demand of the product (e.g. the box must survive stacking six-deep in transit). Avoid vague answers such as ‘it is strong’ without specifying the type of strength and why it matters for that particular application.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Material selection balances function, aesthetics, cost, availability and environmental factors; no single material wins on every criterion and selection always involves a justified compromise.
  • ISO A-series sizes follow the 1:√2 aspect ratio so two sheets of any size form the next size up. Corrugation and lamination are the primary structural strategies for stiffening boards; grain direction must be oriented correctly at fold lines.
  • Sustainable selection means specifying FSC certification, recycled content or recyclable end-of-life options. Foil-lined boards offer superior barrier performance but are difficult to recycle; designers should weigh this against the food-waste benefit they provide.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer specifying packaging for a range of chilled ready meals might choose foil-lined board over standard folding boxboard.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Chilled ready meals contain moisture and require protection from oxygen to prevent spoilage, which standard folding boxboard cannot provide.
- Foil-lined board has an aluminium layer that acts as a barrier to both moisture vapour and oxygen, extending shelf life.
- The foil layer also provides a degree of insulation, helping to maintain the chilled temperature of the product during short periods outside refrigeration.
- Folding boxboard alone would allow moisture to migrate through the board, causing the carton to weaken and the product to deteriorate faster. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain, with reference to specific material properties, how a designer would select a board for a luxury perfume carton, considering both performance and aesthetic requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Solid white board (SWB) would be selected for its brilliant white surface on both sides, ensuring that printed brand colours appear vivid and accurate.
- SWB is made entirely from bleached chemical pulp, giving it higher stiffness per unit of thickness than recycled-content boards, so the carton holds its shape on the shelf.
- A high-gloss or soft-touch laminate finish applied to the outer surface enhances the tactile quality of the carton, reinforcing the premium brand positioning.
- UV spot varnish or foil blocking on the logo adds a visual highlight that differentiates the product at point of sale.
- Cost is a secondary consideration for luxury packaging; the higher cost of SWB is justified by the elevated retail price of the perfume.
[6 marks - Mastering: Properties linked to both functional performance and aesthetic outcome with specific reference to the luxury context. Secure: Properties identified with some linkage to aesthetics or performance but without full development. Developing: Correct board named; limited justification. practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of specifying recycled-content board for a food packaging carton, considering functional, aesthetic and environmental factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages:
- Using recycled fibre reduces the demand for virgin wood pulp, conserving forest resources and reducing carbon emissions associated with timber harvesting and chemical pulping.
- Recycled-content board can be certified and carry on-pack environmental claims (e.g. recycled content percentage) that appeal to eco-conscious consumers and major retailers.
- It is typically cheaper than virgin-fibre board, reducing the unit cost of the packaging and improving commercial viability.
- Recycled fibre can provide adequate structural performance for many food carton applications, such as cereal or cracker boxes, where extreme stiffness is not required.
Disadvantages:
- Shortened fibres in recycled board reduce tensile strength and stiffness, which can be a problem for packaging that must withstand heavy stacking in a warehouse.
- The grey or brown colour of recycled board requires a white-coated top surface to achieve a printable base, adding cost and reducing the net environmental benefit.
- Residual ink or contaminants in the recycled stream may affect food safety if the board is in direct contact with food, requiring an additional barrier liner.
- Consumer perception of recycled board as lower quality may undermine premium brand positioning for high-value food products.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion across functional, aesthetic and environmental dimensions with at least two developed points on each side. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

lessons.title: Shaping & Converting Papers & Boards
lessons.description: Commercial and workshop processes for cutting, creasing, perforating and forming paper and board products.
lessons.content_html:
From Flat Sheet to Finished Form

Paper and board arrive from the mill as flat sheets or rolls. Converting them into three-dimensional packaging, displays or printed components requires a series of converting processes. These processes fall into two broad categories: commercial processes used in high-volume industrial production, and workshop processes used during design development and small-batch manufacture. Understanding both is essential: the commercial process determines what is technically possible at scale, while workshop processes allow designers to prototype and test ideas before committing to expensive tooling.

Nets and Developments for Packaging

Before any cutting or creasing can take place, the designer must produce a net (also called a development). A net shows every face of the finished 3D form laid out flat, with fold lines, glue tabs and cut lines clearly marked. Accuracy is critical: a net that is even 1 mm out will produce a carton that will not close correctly or whose glued joints do not align. Designers draw nets by hand with instruments, or more commonly using CAD software that can export files directly to cutting equipment. Standard nets for tuck-end cartons, crash-lock bases and sealed-end boxes are well established, but complex structural forms (e.g. a display tray with integral dividers) require bespoke development.

Key Fact

A net is a flat template that folds into a 3D form. All faces must be joined edge-to-edge in the correct sequence, with scored fold lines, cut edges and glue tabs accurately positioned. Drawing and testing a net by hand before committing to commercial tooling is a standard step in professional packaging design.

Die Cutting

Die cutting is the primary commercial method for cutting and creasing packaging nets from board. A steel-rule die is made by bending thin strips of hardened steel (the ‘rules’) into the shape of the net and embedding them in a plywood base. The die contains two types of rule: sharp cutting rules that slice cleanly through the board, and blunt creasing rules (slightly lower) that compress the board fibres without cutting, forming a fold line. When the die is pressed against the sheet under high pressure, the entire net is cut and creased in a single operation. Die cutting produces very precise, repeatable results at high speed — a typical carton-board die-cutter can process tens of thousands of sheets per hour. The initial cost of the die is high, making die cutting economical only at large production volumes.

Creasing and Scoring

A crease is produced by compressing the board fibres along the fold line; a score is a partial cut that penetrates part way through the board thickness. Both methods create a clean, accurate fold. Creasing is preferred for thicker boards because it does not weaken the structure; scoring is common for thinner boards and papers where clean folding is needed without a mechanical press. In workshop conditions, scoring is done with a bone folder or the back of a scalpel blade run against a metal rule. Correct creasing and scoring are essential — a crease made against the grain direction will crack the surface coating and weaken the fold.

Perforating and Kiss Cutting

Perforating creates a line of small holes through a sheet so that a panel or strip can be cleanly torn away by the user — common on tear-off coupons, postage stamps and food packaging windows. Kiss cutting is a specialist die-cutting technique used for self-adhesive labels and stickers: the cutting rule penetrates through the face paper and adhesive layer but stops short of cutting through the backing paper. This leaves the label attached to the backing sheet, ready for peeling, while the backing remains intact for handling and dispensing through automatic label applicators. Kiss cutting requires precise control of the cutting depth, typically to within 0.02 mm.

Key Fact

In die cutting, the die contains both cutting rules (sharp, full-depth) and creasing rules (blunt, shallower). Both are embedded in the same plywood base and pressed simultaneously, so a single stroke of the press produces a fully cut and creased net ready for folding. This efficiency makes die cutting the dominant commercial process for high-volume carton production.

Laser Cutting

Laser cutting uses a focused beam of light (typically a CO&sub2; laser) to vaporise or burn through paper, board or foam board along a digitally defined path. Unlike die cutting, it requires no tooling — the cutting path is defined entirely in software and can be changed instantly for each job. This makes laser cutting ideal for prototyping, short runs and complex curved shapes that would be expensive to produce with a steel-rule die. Laser cutting is precise to fractions of a millimetre and can also be used for engraving (partial-depth burning to create a decorative or tactile surface finish) and vector scoring. Drawbacks include a relatively slow cutting speed compared with die cutting, and the burn marks and slight charring of cut edges that can be visible on light-coloured boards.

Guillotining

A guillotine cuts a stack of sheets to a precise straight edge using a long, powered blade. Commercial guillotines can process a ream or more of paper at a single stroke, making them efficient for trimming printed sheets to final size. In a workshop, a handheld guillotine or a rotary trimmer cuts individual sheets accurately. Guillotines produce only straight cuts — they cannot produce curves or complex shapes — so they are used for squaring sheets before printing or trimming after printing, not for producing final product shapes. Safety is critical: all modern commercial guillotines have two-hand operation guards to prevent accidental hand injuries.

In a school workshop or design studio, paper and board are worked with hand tools. A scalpel with a fresh blade and a metal safety rule cuts accurately along straight lines without tearing. A steel rule is mandatory — cutting against a plastic rule risks the blade jumping into the fingers. A cutting mat protects the worksurface and keeps the blade sharp. A bone folder or blunt scoring tool run along a metal rule creates a clean crease before folding. Scissors are suitable for lighter papers but produce a rougher edge on card and are difficult to control for straight lines. Circle cutters and compass cutters allow accurate circular cuts that a scalpel cannot easily achieve.

Foam board requires a long blade in the scalpel or a dedicated foam-board cutter to cut cleanly through the polystyrene core in a single pass. Multiple passes with a short blade tend to tear the core rather than cut it cleanly. Corrugated card is best cut with a strong craft knife rather than scissors, as the fluted core compresses under scissor pressure and produces a ragged edge.

Folding and Assembling Nets

Once a net has been cut and creased, it is assembled by folding along the crease lines and applying adhesive to the glue tabs. In commercial production, this is done by automatic folding-and-gluing machines that can fold and glue a carton in a fraction of a second. In workshop or prototype production, the designer folds and glues by hand using a PVA adhesive, double-sided tape or a glue stick. The sequence of folds matters: most tuck-end cartons are assembled side-glue-tab first, then the base is closed before the product is inserted and the top tuck flap is closed last.

Die cutting is fast, highly precise and economical at large volumes, but the steel-rule die costs hundreds of pounds to produce and cannot be changed once made. Laser cutting has no tooling cost and can be modified instantly but is slow and leaves charred edges. Guillotining is fast for straight cuts but cannot produce shapes. For a design student producing a prototype, laser cutting or hand tools are the practical options; for a manufacturer making 100,000 cartons, die cutting is the only economically viable choice. Understanding these trade-offs allows a designer to recommend the appropriate process for a given production context.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to describe a cutting or converting process, include three elements: what the process does (e.g. cuts and creases simultaneously), how it works (e.g. a steel-rule die pressed under high pressure), and when it is appropriate (e.g. high-volume commercial production). Avoid mixing up die cutting (cuts and creases in one operation) with guillotining (straight cuts only) or laser cutting (no tooling, software-controlled path). Questions about nets should always mention fold lines, glue tabs and cut edges as distinct elements.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A net is a flat template with cut lines, scored or creased fold lines and glue tabs that assembles into a 3D form; accuracy is critical because even small errors prevent a carton from closing correctly.
  • Die cutting uses a steel-rule die to cut and crease in one operation at high speed; laser cutting requires no tooling and suits prototyping and short runs; guillotining produces only straight cuts for trimming sheets.
  • Kiss cutting penetrates only to the backing paper, leaving self-adhesive labels attached for peeling; perforating creates tear lines; creasing compresses fibres for a clean fold without cutting through.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using laser cutting compared with die cutting for producing packaging nets in a small design studio.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of laser cutting:
- No tooling cost: the cutting path is defined entirely in software, so there is no need to invest in a steel-rule die, which can cost hundreds of pounds.
- Designs can be modified instantly between cuts, making it ideal for iterative prototyping where the net shape is still being refined.
- Capable of cutting intricate curves and complex shapes that would be difficult or expensive to produce with a die.
- A single machine can cut and engrave different jobs without any changeover time.
Disadvantages of laser cutting:
- Slow throughput: the laser traces each cutting path sequentially, making it impractical for production quantities above a few hundred units.
- Charring and burn marks on cut edges can affect the appearance of light-coloured or white boards, requiring sanding or masking.
- The machine has a high purchase and maintenance cost, although shared facilities (e.g. a school workshop or fabrication lab) reduce the per-use cost.
- Cutting thicker boards (e.g. 5 mm foam board) may require multiple passes, reducing accuracy and increasing processing time.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion with at least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages relevant to a small design studio context. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

lessons.title: Printing & Finishing
lessons.description: Commercial printing processes and surface finishes that protect, enhance and differentiate paper and board products.
lessons.content_html:
Why Printing and Finishing Matter

A perfectly constructed carton with no print is worthless at point of sale. Printing communicates brand identity, product information, legal requirements and visual appeal. Finishing — applying a coating, texture or foil over the printed surface — adds protection, elevates perceived quality and can make a product physically stand out on a shelf. Together, printing and finishing are the processes that transform a blank piece of board into the persuasive, durable, eye-catching packaging or graphic product a designer has conceived. Understanding these processes allows a designer to specify them correctly in a manufacturing brief and to appreciate why they cost what they do.

Offset Lithography

Offset lithography is the world’s most widely used commercial printing process for paper and board. It exploits the principle that oil and water repel each other. A printing plate (typically aluminium, around 0.3 mm thick) is chemically treated so that image areas attract oil-based ink and reject water, while non-image areas attract water and reject ink. The inked image is then transferred (‘offset’) from the plate to a rubber blanket cylinder, and from there to the paper or board. The rubber blanket conforms to the surface of the substrate, giving sharper results than direct plate-to-paper printing. Full-colour printing uses four plates in sequence: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (Black) — the CMYK process. Each colour is printed as a pattern of microscopic halftone dots; the eye blends them to produce the full spectrum of visible colours. Lithography is cost-effective at runs of several thousand sheets upward, producing consistent, high-quality results at high speed.

Screen Printing

Screen printing forces ink through a fine mesh screen onto the substrate. Areas of the screen that should not print are blocked with a photochemically applied stencil; ink is pushed through open mesh areas with a rubber squeegee. Each colour requires a separate screen. Screen printing deposits a thick, opaque layer of ink, producing vivid, high-impact colours that are ideal for printing on dark or textured substrates. Unlike lithography, screen printing works on rigid, three-dimensional objects as well as flat sheets — bottles, tins, clothing and circuit boards can all be screen-printed. It is economical for short runs or for applications requiring specialist inks (fluorescent, metallic, UV-reactive, conductive) that cannot be used in a litho press.

Flexography

Flexography uses a flexible polymer relief plate mounted on a rotating cylinder. Image areas are raised above the non-image surface and pick up ink from an anilox roller (a cylinder engraved with tiny cells that control ink volume). The inked image is then printed directly onto the substrate. Flexographic inks dry very rapidly by evaporation or UV curing, making the process suited to continuous-feed production lines. Flexography is the dominant process for printing on corrugated board, plastic carrier bags, food wrappers and newspaper supplements — any application requiring fast drying on a non-absorbent or structurally delicate substrate. Print quality is slightly lower than lithography, particularly for fine detail and photographic images.

Digital and Inkjet Printing

Digital printing — including large-format inkjet and electrostatic toner-based printing — requires no printing plates. The image is sent directly from a computer file to the print engine, where microscopic droplets of CMYK (and sometimes additional) inks are jetted or fused onto the substrate. The key advantages are zero set-up cost (no plates to make), instant changeover between different designs, and the ability to personalise each sheet differently (variable data printing). These properties make digital printing ideal for short runs, prototypes and personalised packaging. The main limitations are higher cost per unit at large volumes compared with lithography, and restrictions on the range of substrates and inks that can be used. Large-format inkjet printers are standard in school design departments and commercial sign-making workshops.

Key Fact

Full-colour offset lithography uses four ink colours: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (Black) — abbreviated CMYK. Each colour is printed separately as halftone dots. Where all four overlap at full density, the result is a near-black. The eye blends the dots at normal reading distance to perceive continuous tones and millions of intermediate colours from just four inks.

Varnishing

Varnish is a clear liquid coating applied over a printed surface to protect the ink from abrasion, moisture and fingerprints, and to enhance the visual finish. Gloss varnish reflects light, making colours appear brighter and more saturated. Matt varnish absorbs light, giving a flat, sophisticated appearance with low glare. Satin (or silk) varnish sits between the two extremes. Varnish can be applied over the entire sheet (flood varnish) or selectively over specific design elements using a printing plate (spot varnish). UV spot varnish is applied to a precise area and instantly cured by ultraviolet light, creating a high-gloss, raised tactile effect. A common technique is soft-touch varnish, which creates a velvety, almost rubberised surface texture that feels luxurious and discourages fingerprinting.

Lamination

Lamination bonds a thin transparent film (typically biaxially-oriented polypropylene, BOPP) to the printed surface using heat and pressure or adhesive. Like varnish, it is available in gloss, matt and satin finishes. Lamination offers considerably more protection than varnish — it is waterproof, scuff-resistant and significantly increases the structural stiffness of the board. For this reason, lamination is the standard finish for hardback book covers, premium food packaging, folded leaflets and retail bags. The main environmental drawback is that laminated paper and board is more difficult to recycle, as the plastic film must be separated from the fibre.

Key Fact

UV spot varnish is applied selectively to specific design elements (e.g. a logo or product image) and cured instantly by ultraviolet light. The result is a high-gloss, slightly raised area that contrasts with the surrounding matt or satin finish, drawing the eye and the fingertip to the key visual element. This technique is widely used on premium packaging, luxury brochures and book covers.

Embossing and Debossing

Embossing uses a matched pair of male and female metal dies pressed together with the board between them, raising a design element above the surface in relief. Debossing uses the same principle but presses the image into the surface, creating a sunken impression. Both processes can be done blind (no ink or foil, relying on the shadow and highlight of the relief) or combined with foil blocking. Embossing is used on premium packaging, business cards and stationery to add a tactile quality that immediately communicates high value.

Foil Blocking

Foil blocking (also called hot foil stamping) uses a heated metal die to press a thin metallic foil onto the surface of the board. Under heat and pressure, the foil transfers from its carrier film to the board surface. Gold, silver, holographic and coloured foils are all available. Foil blocking produces a brilliant, mirror-like metallic finish that cannot be achieved by printing with metallic ink alone. It is used on luxury product packaging, book covers, greetings cards and security documents. Foil blocking can be combined with embossing in a single press operation for maximum visual and tactile impact.

Every surface finish serves one or more of three purposes: protection, aesthetics and function. Gloss lamination on a food-service menu protects the print from food and liquid spills (protection), makes colours appear brighter (aesthetics) and allows the surface to be wiped clean (function). UV spot varnish on a luxury perfume carton adds no measurable protection but dramatically improves visual appeal at point of sale (pure aesthetics). Foil blocking on a security document provides a holographic element that is difficult to counterfeit (function). Designers must specify finishes with clear reasons linked to the product’s performance requirements, not just because they ‘look nice’.

Cost also determines finish choice: flood lamination adds approximately 5–15% to the print cost; UV spot varnish is more expensive per unit because it requires an additional print pass; foil blocking costs more again because each colour of foil requires a separate die. At low production volumes, digital spot varnish (applied by an inkjet-based digital press) offers a cheaper alternative to UV spot, though with slightly less tactile relief.

Offset lithography: medium-to-high volume, highest quality for paper and board, four-plate CMYK, slow set-up. Screen printing: short-to-medium run, thick opaque ink, specialist substrates including three-dimensional objects. Flexography: continuous-feed, fast-drying inks, lower quality, corrugated and film substrates. Digital/inkjet: very short run or one-offs, no plates, variable data, moderate quality. A question asking you to justify a printing process choice should always reference: volume of production, substrate type, print quality required and set-up cost.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing printing processes in an exam, structure your answer around four criteria: volume (short, medium, long run), substrate (paper, board, film, 3D object), quality (photographic detail, flat colour) and cost (set-up vs unit cost). For finishing questions, always state why a finish is applied — protection, aesthetics or function — and link it to a specific product context. Writing ‘lamination makes it shiny’ misses the point; ‘gloss lamination protects the printed surface from scuffing during transit and increases perceived quality at point of sale’ answers correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four main commercial printing processes are offset lithography (high-volume, CMYK, highest quality), screen printing (short run, thick ink, 3D substrates), flexography (continuous-feed, corrugated and film packaging) and digital inkjet (no plates, short run, variable data).
  • Surface finishes include varnishing (gloss, matt, UV spot), lamination (waterproof film bonded over print), embossing and debossing (tactile relief via metal dies) and foil blocking (metallic transfer under heat and pressure).
  • Every finish serves a defined purpose: protection (lamination on a menu), aesthetics (UV spot on a perfume carton) or function (holographic foil on a security document). Designers must justify finish choices against the product brief, not just visual preference.

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between gloss lamination and UV spot varnish as surface finishing techniques, including why each is applied and the effect each produces on a printed carton.

Students may include:

- UV spot varnish is applied selectively to specific areas of the printed design, creating a high-gloss, slightly raised tactile contrast against the surrounding surface.
- Lamination is primarily functional: it protects the surface from moisture, abrasion and handling, making it suitable for products that experience heavy use (menus, carrier bags, brochure covers).
- UV spot varnish is primarily aesthetic: it creates a premium visual and tactile quality by highlighting key design elements such as logos or product images.

[6 marks - Mastering: Both processes fully described and contrasted in terms of application method, purpose and carton context. Secure: Both described with some contrast; purpose linked but not fully developed. Developing: One process well described; second superficial. Emerging: Vague reference to one process only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using offset lithography compared with screen printing for producing 50,000 units of printed retail packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of offset lithography:
- Produces the highest quality photographic image reproduction via CMYK halftone dot printing, suitable for detailed product photography on packaging.
- At 50,000 units, the fixed cost of making four printing plates is easily amortised across the run, giving a very low cost per sheet.
- High-speed rotary presses can print thousands of sheets per hour, meeting a tight production schedule.
- Consistent, repeatable colour across the entire run is maintained by ink density controls, important for brand colour accuracy.
Disadvantages of offset lithography:
- Four plates must be made for a full-colour job, adding a significant set-up cost that makes it uneconomical for short runs.
- Lithography works best on flat sheets of paper and board; it cannot easily print onto corrugated or three-dimensional substrates.
- Any design change (e.g. a regulatory update on food packaging) requires a new plate, adding cost and delay.
Advantages of screen printing at 50,000 units:
- Screen printing deposits a thick, opaque ink layer that can print on dark or textured boards where lithography would produce dull, washed-out colours.
- Specialist inks (metallic, UV-reactive, tactile) can be used in screen printing that are not compatible with lithographic presses.
Disadvantages:
- Screen printing is significantly slower than lithography and more expensive per unit at high volumes, making 50,000 units costly.
- Each colour requires a separate screen set-up, and fine photographic detail is harder to achieve than with lithographic halftone dots.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced comparison with at least two developed points for each process, linked to the 50,000-unit context. Secure: Two points per process with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

lessons.title: Commercial Production, Sustainability & Applications
lessons.description: Scales of production, the 6 Rs applied to paper and board, and modern developments in paper-based products.
lessons.content_html:
Scales of Production for Paper and Board Products

Paper and board products are manufactured at every scale, from a single prototype to billions of units per year. Understanding the appropriate scale of production is essential for selecting the right processes, tooling and materials. Designers specify products with a target production volume in mind from the earliest stages of development — a process only appropriate at high volumes (e.g. die cutting) should not be specified for a short run, and vice versa.

  • One-off production — a single unique item made by hand or using digital tools (laser cutter, inkjet printer). Examples include a bespoke presentation box for an award ceremony or a prototype packaging mock-up. Very high cost per unit; skilled labour is the main expense.
  • Batch production — a set quantity of identical items produced together, then the production line is reconfigured for a different product. A print run of 500 corporate brochures or 2,000 seasonal point-of-sale displays are typical examples. Set-up costs are shared across the batch, giving a moderate unit cost.
  • Mass production — continuous, high-volume manufacture of a single product design, typically using dedicated automated lines. Cereal boxes, drinks cartons and newspaper inserts are produced in the tens or hundreds of millions. Automation minimises labour cost; the unit cost is extremely low but the capital investment is enormous.
  • Continuous production — an uninterrupted process that runs 24 hours a day, producing a continuous output (e.g. the paper mill itself, which runs constantly to justify the energy cost of maintaining operating temperatures). The paper web never stops — roll changes happen without stopping the machine.
Key Fact

In mass production of cartons, a fully automated line feeds board through a printer, die cutter and folding-and-gluing machine in a single continuous pass. The speed of a modern carton-filling line is measured in hundreds of cartons per minute. Any stoppage costs the manufacturer thousands of pounds, so quality control systems (including camera-based vision systems that reject defective cartons) run in real time alongside production.

The 6 Rs Applied to Papers and Boards

The 6 Rs (Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Repair) provide a structured framework for evaluating the environmental performance of paper and board products throughout their lifecycle — from raw material to end of life.

  • Rethink — question whether the product needs to exist in its current form. Could a paper bag replace a plastic bag? Could a digital communication replace a printed brochure? Rethinking upstream decisions can eliminate environmental impact entirely rather than just mitigating it.
  • Refuse — decline to use materials or processes with a disproportionate environmental cost when an adequate alternative exists. A designer might refuse to specify foil-lined laminated board where a simpler recyclable board would meet the performance requirement.
  • Reduce — use less material. Lightweight packaging (source reduction) is the packaging industry’s primary sustainability strategy: thinning the board gauge, minimising glue tab sizes and optimising net shapes to reduce offcuts all reduce material consumption and transport weight simultaneously.
  • Reuse — design the product so it can serve a second function after its primary use. A rigid gift box with a magnetic lid can be reused for storage; a premium carrier bag with rope handles can become a shopping bag for months. Reuse extends the functional life of the materials already invested in the product.
  • Recycle — paper and board are among the most recyclable materials in everyday use. UK recycling rates for paper and board packaging stand above 70%. Fibres can be recycled five to seven times before they become too short to use further. Maximising recyclability means avoiding multi-material laminates, foil layers and plastic coatings that contaminate the recycling stream.
  • Repair — less directly applicable to single-use packaging, but relevant for durable paper-based products such as books, boxes and folders. A well-constructed hardback book, for example, can be re-bound; a quality file box can have a damaged panel replaced rather than discarded.

Recycling, Biodegradability and FSC Certification

Paper and board hold several sustainability advantages over many competing materials. They are biodegradable — when sent to landfill or composted, they break down naturally within months rather than centuries, unlike plastics. They are readily recyclable at scale in well-established infrastructure — kerbside collection for cardboard and paper is near-universal in the UK. Paper and board can also be made from renewable resources (managed forestry), unlike fossil-fuel-derived plastics. FSC certification guarantees that virgin-fibre content comes from forests where replanting matches or exceeds felling rates, maintaining long-term carbon sequestration and biodiversity.

Key Fact

Paper fibre can be recycled five to seven times before the cellulose fibres become too short to bond into a usable sheet. After this point, the fibre exits the material cycle as sludge used in construction materials or as fuel for energy recovery. This means that a piece of paper entering the recycling stream today has already passed through several previous products, and may become several more before its fibre life ends.

Case Study: Food Packaging

A point-of-sale display unit for a supermarket bakery illustrates the range of paper and board materials and processes in a single application. The FSDU (free-standing display unit) uses a corrugated double-wall board base for structural rigidity to support the product weight; the graphics panels are printed duplex board, laminated with a gloss film to protect against grease splashes and to maintain colour vibrancy under retail lighting; and the branded header card at the top uses a solid white board with UV spot varnish on the logo to maximise visibility at a distance. The entire unit is designed to arrive flat-packed and be assembled in-store in under five minutes, requiring no tools. At end of life, the unit is broken down and placed in the retailer’s cardboard recycling stream.

This case study demonstrates how different board types, printing processes and finishes are combined in a single product to meet functional requirements (structural support, grease resistance), aesthetic requirements (colour vibrancy, brand visibility) and end-of-life requirements (flat-pack, recyclable). A design team working on such a brief would produce a material specification for each component, justifying each choice against the performance criteria.

Paper and board are being developed with new functional properties that extend their application into areas traditionally dominated by plastics and metals. Active packaging incorporates functional additives into the board structure — oxygen scavengers absorb residual oxygen inside food cartons to extend shelf life; moisture-regulating coatings maintain humidity inside fresh-produce boxes. Near-field communication (NFC) paper embeds a thin conductive antenna and chip within a paper sheet, enabling a smartphone to read product information, authentication codes or reorder links simply by tapping the packaging — without any visible electronic component on the surface. Thermochromic inks printed onto board packaging change colour at a specific temperature, providing a visual cue that a product has been chilled, heated or has reached a safe serving temperature. These developments address real product performance needs while maintaining the sustainability advantages of paper-based materials.

Structural paper products are also advancing. Moulded pulp packaging — familiar as egg boxes and electronic product inserts — is being refined with smoother surface finishes and tighter dimensional tolerances to replace expanded polystyrene in high-value electronics packaging. Major technology brands have announced commitments to replace all plastic packaging with moulded pulp alternatives by the end of this decade, driven by consumer pressure and extended producer responsibility regulations.

A full lifecycle assessment (LCA) of a paper or board product considers every stage: raw material extraction (timber harvesting, water and chemical use in pulping), manufacturing (energy for drying and calendering), distribution (transport emissions, packaging of the packaging itself), use phase (how long the product is in service, whether it is reused) and end of life (recycled, composted, landfilled or incinerated with energy recovery). Paper and board perform well in most stages compared with plastic alternatives, but the manufacture stage is energy-intensive and water-intensive, and the use phase is often very short for single-use packaging. Designers who understand LCA can make choices — increasing board reuse potential, specifying recycled content, avoiding multi-material laminates — that improve the profile at every stage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When applying the 6 Rs to a paper or board product in the exam, go beyond simply naming each R — demonstrate understanding by linking each principle to a specific design decision that a designer could take. ‘Reduce’ is not enough; ‘reduce the board gauge from 350 g/m² to 300 g/m² to lower material consumption and transport weight without compromising carton integrity’ scores full marks. Sustainability questions that offer 6 or 8 marks always expect developed, applied points, not a list of single-word answers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Paper and board products are made at every scale from one-off prototypes to continuous mass production; the appropriate process, tooling and material depend on the production volume specified in the brief.
  • The 6 Rs (Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair) provide a framework for improving sustainability at every stage; paper and board score well through biodegradability, recyclability (five to seven fibre cycles) and FSC certification for responsible sourcing.
  • Modern developments including active packaging additives, NFC-embedded paper, thermochromic inks and moulded pulp are extending the functional range of paper-based materials, often as sustainable replacements for plastics in packaging.

One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:

practice_questions.text: Explain why FSC certification is important to a designer specifying virgin-fibre board for a product brief.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- FSC certification guarantees that the timber used to make the board was harvested from forests managed to strict environmental standards, where replanting matches or exceeds felling rates.
- This ensures the designer can demonstrate responsible material sourcing to a client who has a sustainability policy or who markets their products on environmental credentials.
- The FSC logo on the finished product provides verifiable evidence of responsible sourcing that consumers and retailers can trust, unlike unverified environmental claims.
- Using FSC-certified board helps maintain long-term forest cover and biodiversity, sequestering carbon and protecting habitats rather than contributing to deforestation. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Using a point-of-sale food packaging display as a context, explain how two different board materials and two different finishing processes could be combined to meet functional, aesthetic and sustainability requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Corrugated double-wall board for the structural base and sides of the display unit provides the compressive strength needed to bear product weight without adding excessive weight to the unit itself.
- Duplex board for the printed graphics panels provides a white, coated printing surface for high-quality brand imagery, at a lower cost and with recycled-content backing compared with solid white board.
- Gloss lamination on the graphics panels protects the print from grease, moisture and handling damage in a busy retail environment, extending the functional life of the display.
- UV spot varnish on the logo and hero product image increases shelf visibility and communicates premium brand values at point of sale.
- Both board types are recyclable at end of life: the display can be broken down into the retailer's cardboard stream, meeting sustainability requirements for a retail client.
[6 marks - Mastering: Two materials and two finishes clearly justified against functional, aesthetic and sustainability requirements with reference to the POS display context. Secure: Two materials or finishes identified with some justification but coverage of all three requirement types incomplete. Developing: One material and one finish described; limited justification. Emerging: Vague material or finish identified with no justification.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of paper and board as packaging materials compared with rigid plastics, considering sustainability, function and consumer perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board are biodegradable and break down naturally within months in landfill or composting conditions, unlike rigid plastics which persist for hundreds of years.
- Paper fibre is recyclable up to five to seven times and is collected and processed through a well-established, near-universal UK kerbside recycling infrastructure, giving high actual recycling rates (above 70% for packaging board).
- Paper and board are made from a renewable resource (managed forestry) certified by bodies such as the FSC, unlike petroleum-based plastics which depend on a finite fossil fuel supply.
- Consumer perception of paper-based packaging is strongly positive; research consistently shows that shoppers associate cardboard packaging with environmental responsibility, which supports brand values in environmentally aware markets.
Disadvantages of paper and board:
- Paper and board provide little barrier to moisture and oxygen without additional coatings or laminates, limiting their use in packaging wet, fatty or oxygen-sensitive products compared with plastics that provide an inherent barrier.
- Rigid plastic packaging is generally lighter per unit volume than board, reducing transport emissions per product; it also offers superior impact protection for fragile goods.
- Multi-material paper and board constructions (foil-lined cartons, laminated board) are difficult to recycle and in practice are often sent to landfill or energy recovery, undermining the recyclability advantage.
- Paper and board packaging typically has a shorter functional life before it loses structural integrity under moisture or handling, whereas rigid plastic containers can be reused many times.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced discussion across sustainability, functional performance and consumer perception with at least two developed points on each side. Secure: Two advantages and two disadvantages identified with some development across at least two of the three dimensions. Developing: Points listed with limited development; coverage of only one dimension. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]
